header:
Date: 2025-11-05
Start: 14:00 PST
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Ortiz (Redwood AE), Riley Chen (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Helios - Security Manager), Darren Cole (Helios - Platform Ops), Marta Ruiz (Helios - Compliance)
summary: Redwood walked Helios through what admin and audit telemetry we capture, export options (S3 export, syslog, webhook streaming), and retention/rotation patterns. Helios clarified required retention windows and legal-hold needs for financial records. Action items: Redwood to send SOC2/ISO evidence pack and sample export manifest; schedule pilot to validate streaming exports to Helios S3/syslog; customer to confirm retention matrix.
topics:
1) What admin events are captured (user logins, role changes, API key ops, workspace/model changes, system-level errors)
2) Export mechanisms (S3 batch export, continuous syslog, webhook, CDC Kafka)
3) Retention/archival and legal hold (90 days default vs 7-year regulatory needs)
4) Encryption and KMS/HSM options (customer-managed keys, rotation, dual control)
5) RBAC/SSO audit trails and identity mappings
6) Evidence packaging for auditors (samples, formats, hashes, chain-of-custody)
transcript:
[00:00] Jamie: Okay thanks everyone for joining, we should be able to run about 50 minutes today, thanks for carving the time. I'm Jamie from Redwood, with Riley on the call, that's our solutions engineer.
[00:08] Aisha: Hi all, Aisha here, security owner for Helios. We're mainly focused on what you retain, how we can pull it out, and proof for audits, like chain of custody and integrity.
[00:20] Riley: Great, thanks Aisha. Quick agenda: capture surface, export options, retention & legal hold, encryption/KMS, and then we close with next steps. Sound right?
[00:28] Darren: Yeah that's right, we have auditors in December so we're trying to lock the playbook.
[00:34] Marta: plus we need to be explicit about evidence formats, CSV vs JSON, checksums, that kind of thing.
[00:40] Riley: Perfect. So first, what we capture — high level — admin actions: user account creates/deletes, role assignments, SAML SSO sessions, token and API key creation/deletion, model publish/rollback, configuration changes to routing/policies, and escalation events. Also system events: scheduler/autoscale failures and node reboots — those are captured but labeled as infra telemetry.
[01:05] Aisha: When you say 'token ops' does that include full token content or just metadata? We cannot have full secrets in logs.
[01:12] Riley: Good point, we never store secret tokens. It's metadata only — actor, operation type, timestamp, request ID, resource id. If a token value is present in an incoming request, it's redacted server-side and we only log a hash for linkage.
[01:28] Aisha: okay that's fine. How long are these retained by default?
[01:31] Jamie: Default retention for admin events in hosted is 90 days, with options to push to your own long-term storage. Dedicated/private can be configured to respect customer retention SLAs.
[01:41] Darren: Our compliance requires 7 years for certain transaction-related admin ops. That means we need export and archiving, and immutable storage with checksums.
[01:50] Riley: Yep, we support a couple of export mechanisms: periodic batch exports to your S3 or GCS bucket (daily/weekly), continuous streaming to syslog/ELK via our syslog forwarder, and webhook/Kafka CDC style pushes for real-time ingestion. There is also a log-archive snapshot we can produce on demand — basically a time-limited snapshot with manifest and SHA256 checksums.
[02:11] Marta: Tell me more about the manifest and chain-of-custody. Auditors want proof the logs weren't tampered with.
[02:17] Riley: For each snapshot we produce a manifest (JSON) that lists files, sizes, sha256 hashes, a signed metadata file using Redwood's internal signing key, and optionally we can provide a signed timestamp from an external timestamper. If you'd prefer, we can encrypt the archive with your KMS key and provide the key wrap metadata so you have exclusive decrypt.
[02:40] Aisha: Signing with your key is fine but we prefer customer-managed keys where possible, especially for older archives — can Redwood support CMK or HSM integration?
[02:48] Jamie: Yes, for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) and HSMs for on-prem. For Hosted we offer a bring-your-own-key flow for snapshot encryption — the archive is encrypted client-side using a key you rotate; Redwood never sees plaintext. We also support envelope encryption when pushing to S3.
[03:10] Darren: How about key rotation — do you rotate the signing keys? What's your retention of the signing key history for verification in future audits?
[03:16] Riley: Redwood rotates internal signing keys on a regular schedule (annually or on-demand for incidents). We keep an archived chain-of-trust mapping so when we sign a manifest we also include the signing key ID and certificate chain. If you bring your own keys, you manage rotation and we store only the wrapped key metadata.
[03:33] Marta: Are audit exports tamper-evident if sent to our S3? If someone deletes files from the bucket accidentally, what's the recovery model?
[03:40] Riley: For S3 we strongly recommend using immutable object lock / retention policies and cross-region replication for durability. On top of that, we provide manifests and checksums so you can detect deletion or modification. If you use Glacier-like storage, we can provide a rehydration playbook. For accidental deletes, typical recovery is via your cloud provider's object versioning or backup. Redwood can also keep an internal cold snapshot for a limited window upon request.
[04:06] Aisha: Okay good. On the RBAC/SSO side, we need to map Redwood roles to our internal roles so auditors can see who had what permissions when an action occurred. How granular are your role change events?
[04:16] Riley: We log role change events with before/after state, actor, and request ID. The logs include human-readable role names and internal role IDs. We also capture role inheritance events, e.g., when a team inherits model access through a policy.
[04:28] Aisha: Do you capture the SAML assertion id so we can tie a login to an external identity provider?
[04:33] Riley: We capture assertion id and the issuer field, but not the full SAML payload. We can store the assertion id and the subject name id to link back to your IdP logs.
[04:42] Darren: For our legal hold workflows, we need the ability to flag a stream and prevent automatic purging. Does Redwood support an immutable hold flag per-resource?
[04:50] Jamie: Yes, in Dedicated/private we can set retention windows per workspace and support legal hold — preventing automated deletion until release. In hosted we offer a hold workflow via customer support request and an API to tag artifacts for hold; depending on plan we can automate that as well.
[05:05] Marta: If we ask for a snapshot for an audit, how quickly can we get it? We might need a same-day extraction with checksums.
[05:12] Riley: For standard requests, we can produce a snapshot within 24 hours. For expedited requests there's a rush option — depends on the size but often same-day for small-to-medium footprint customers. We'll include a manifest and signed metadata.
[05:24] Aisha: Are there PII redaction features or field-level filters? Some events include user-provided content pointers and we need to avoid capturing PII in logs.
[05:33] Riley: We have configurable scrubbing filters that can redact or hash specific fields in events before they're stored. You can supply a list of fields or regex patterns. For higher-sensitivity tenants we recommend private deployment or dedicated which keeps the runtime isolated and gives you more control over scrubbing rules.
[05:48] Darren: On the exports side, what's the throughput and cost considerations if we stream every admin event in real-time to our SIEM?
[05:56] Riley: Admin events are generally low-volume compared to application logs, but throughput depends on activity level. For continuous syslog streaming we support batching and backpressure — if your SIEM gets overwhelmed we can buffer and publish in bursts. We can also do a filter layer so only high-priority events stream in real time and lower-priority ones go to batch export. We'll share config suggestions based on your event profiles.
[06:18] Aisha: For the evidence pack, auditors will want policy docs: retention policy, change control, key rotation policy, access logs for the signing keys. Can you include those?
[06:29] Jamie: Absolutely, we'll include SOC2/ISO artifacts: access control policies, key mgmt SOPs, change control logs for the service, and sample audit exports. We'll redact anything customer-specific unless you authorize sharing.
[06:39] Marta: I want an example of the JSON manifest format. Does it have a version? We need reproducibility for future audits.
[06:46] Riley: Yes manifests are versioned. We'll attach a schema and an example with the evidence pack. Each manifest includes schema version, generated_at, files listing with hashes, signing metadata (key id, signature), and optional encryption metadata if archived with a customer key.
[07:02] Darren: How do you handle cross-account access for the S3 export? We need to minimize access footprint — ideally Redwood writes into a pre-signed bucket path without assuming a role indefinitely.
[07:11] Riley: Common pattern is either Redwood assumes a short-lived role in your account or we do customer-side pull via pre-signed URLs. For push model we prefer assuming a role with limited time-bound permissions and audited role usage; for pull, we create a pre-signed manifest URL you can fetch. We'll show both options in the runbook.
[07:29] Aisha: Regarding GDPR and data residency, some of our records must reside in EU for EU customers. Can you scope exports by region or tenant?
[07:38] Jamie: Yes. Exports can be region-scoped; we support exporting only EU-region logs and we can place archives in your EU bucket. For Private deployments you control region and physical location. We'll need a mapping of which tenants/organizations require EU residency.
[07:52] Marta: Does Redwood provide proof of deletion for purged records? We need an auditable trail when data is destructed.
[07:58] Riley: We emit deletion events with before/after metadata and a deletion manifest that includes the deleted file/object names and deletion timestamps. If you use immutable object lock we can also include retention-release evidence.
[08:12] Aisha: On the SSO audit side, auditors often ask for a chain showing when admin privileges were granted and used. Can you show a timeline for a principal: when granted, when elevated, and when used?
[08:22] Riley: We can generate a timeline view. Because we log role change events, token generation, and action events with request IDs, we can link and produce a human-readable timeline for a principal over a given window. We'll provide an example in the evidence pack.
[08:36] Darren: For long-term archival we may want to keep an offline signed copy. Is Redwood willing to sign and hand over a copy for retention in our vaults?
[08:44] Jamie: Yes, we can provide signed archives for you to store in a vault. For hosted customers we sign with our certificate; for Private customers you can sign with your own KMS prior to upload.
[08:55] Marta: A nit: audits often want to see who accessed signing key metadata. Is that protected?
[09:00] Riley: Access to signing key metadata is limited; it's part of our control plane audit. We can include the control plane access logs as part of the evidence pack, with role-scoped redaction if needed.
[09:12] Aisha: Okay, let's walk through a hypothetical: auditor requests admin logs for user X between Jan 1 and Jan 31, 2025 — what do you deliver?
[09:20] Riley: We generate a snapshot for that date range, include a manifest, signature, and optionally encrypt with your CMK. We also include the timeline view for the user, raw event files in compressed JSONL, and a verification script to run sha256 checks.
[09:37] Darren: Great. Anything we should be aware of for latency when exporting large ranges?
[09:42] Riley: For large date ranges it's a heavy IO job — time depends on size. We recommend doing incremental exports (weekly) for normal ops and ad-hoc snapshots for audits. For the pilot we'll scope a small window to measure throughput.
[09:54] Jamie: Quick recap then: Redwood to share evidence pack + manifest example and runbook, set up a pilot streaming to Helios S3/syslog, Helios to share retention matrix and list of audit timelines. Any other open questions?
[10:08] Marta: One more: SLA around export availability — if you promise a 24-hour snapshot window, what's the SLA and remediation?
[10:16] Jamie: We'll include SLA language in the evidence pack; typical enterprise SLA includes a 24-hour fulfillment target and credits for missed commitments. We'll surface exact terms in the contract addendum.
[10:27] Aisha: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[10:29] Riley: Thanks, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[10:32] Jamie: End meeting.

Notes on transcription: occasional words garbled (e.g., 'timestamper' sometimes transcribed as 'time stamper'), speaker turns compressed in a few places, natural filler words left intact.
notes: Mentioned export patterns: S3 push (assume role or pre-signed), continuous syslog, webhook/Kafka CDC. Discussed manifests with sha256, signing metadata, signed timestamps, CMK envelope encryption. Discussed legal hold, immutable S3 object lock, role mapping, SAML assertion ids, redaction filters, retention windows (90 days default vs 7 years required), evidence pack deliverables and a pilot for streaming exports.
